# Metta Sutta (Snp 1.8 (PTS Snp 25))

**ID:** Snp 1.8 (PTS Snp 25)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Metta Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Metta Sutta* (Snp 1.8; PTS Snp 25), also widely designated as the *Karaṇīyametta Sutta* after its opening word *karaṇīya* ("what should be done"), is a short poetic discourse preserved in the *Suttanipāta* [Crosby 2014; Williams 2005]. Composed in the Old Āryā metre, the text comprises ten four-line stanzas [symposium2013; Crosby 2014]. It outlines the cultivation of universal loving-kindness (*mettā*): beginning with the foundational virtues and ethical disposition of one skilled in welfare (*attha-kusala*), articulating the attitude of boundless goodwill toward all living beings likened to a mother protecting her only child with her life, and describing the meditative and moral trajectory culminating in freedom from rebirth and the attainment of awakening [symposium2013; Crosby 2014].

The sutta is celebrated across the Theravāda tradition as both a core contemplative text and a primary protective chant (*paritta* or *pirit*) recited to ward off danger, dispel fear, and invoke blessings [Williams & Ladwig 2012; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Crosby 2014]. It forms an indispensable component of daily lay and monastic recitation and school curricula in Sri Lanka [symposium2013; Gombrich, Compassion as means to Nirvana], features regularly in Southeast Asian liturgical practice such as funeral and monastic chanting in Laos and Thailand [Williams & Ladwig 2012], and continues to be chanted in both Pali and English translation in contemporary diaspora communities [Azzopardi 2010].

A complete canonical duplicate is preserved in the *Khuddakapāṭha* under the title *Mettā Sutta* (Kp 9 / PTS Kp 8) [Anālayo 2018; Crosby 2014]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus confirms this verbatim overlap across the entire discourse (§0.2–10.5 ↔ §0.1–11.1), while also registering extensive textual matches in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Caturārakkhadīpanī* [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus identifies cross-language alignments with Sanskrit and Tibetan works, including the Tibetan *Aṣṭādaśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* (D0010) and the Sanskrit *Svastyayanagāthā* [DharmaNexus].
